claims.text: Tuning energy input to reduce all metal precursors simultaneously enables formation of homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Simultaneous precursor reduction synchronizes nucleation events.
Synchronized nucleation promotes uniform atomic mixing.
Asynchronous reduction leads to phase separation and elemental segregation.
The rate of energy input controls the reduction kinetics of the metal components.
Simultaneous reduction produces uniform nucleation sites that mediate atomic mixing.
Concurrent nucleation allows homogeneous mixing to occur before diffusion-driven segregation.
Staggered reduction produces separate nucleation events.
Separate nucleation events cause phase separation and uncontrolled morphology.
Energy conditions promoting synchronized reduction will produce a single-phase alloy with uniform elemental distribution.
Energy conditions promoting synchronized reduction will improve surface-atom exposure relative to conventional energy input.
Energy conditions promoting synchronized reduction will lower decomposition temperature relative to conventional energy input.
Observable phase segregation and elemental clustering will correlate with asynchronous reduction.
Nanoparticles produced using conventional energy input typically have mixed phases and uncontrolled morphology because of asynchronous reduction kinetics.
The proposed mechanism applies to systems containing at least five noble-metal components when their reduction-potential differences are moderate enough to be synchronized by energy-input tuning.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when reduction potentials differ extremely or precursor formulations introduce additional kinetic barriers.
Earlier comparative evidence supports a role for synchronized reduction in successful alloy formation.
The degree of synchronization required and the mechanism's applicability across all noble-metal systems are undetermined.
